ops.title: darwin kern.proc.pid returns EIO, not ESRCH, for a missing PID
ops.body:
**Platform fact, greppable**: on macOS, `unix.SysctlKinfoProc("kern.proc.pid", pid)` answers a PID that does not exist with **EIO** — not the ESRCH every instinct and man page reaches for. Verified empirically 2026-08-04 (go1.26.5, x/sys v0.47.0): absent pids 99998 / 65535 / 1<<30 / -1 all return `input/output error`; `pid 0` succeeds (self). Any consumer that classifies this syscall's errors by errno will misread ordinary absence.

**The design rule this bought (lead with this)**: *prefer an enumeration that is authoritative about absence over per-item probes classified by errno.* A `kern.proc.all` snapshot that returns is authoritative about every PID absent from it — absence versus probe-failure is separated structurally rather than by an errno taxonomy that varies per platform and per call. A failed enumeration then refuses the whole operation before anything is classified, which is a stronger fail-closed than any per-item verdict. Reference implementation: internal/daemon/crossera_terminals.go (`processSnapshot` / `snapshotProcessTable`), commit 72f7c31.

**How the defect happened (first person, ccpool-daemon)**: the legacy-terminal sweep classified liveness per record with kern.proc.pid, treating only ESRCH as definitive absence and everything else as undetermined-refuse. Under EIO, every record whose process had simply exited — the ordinary upgrade, where the old login closed cleanly and left its row behind — classified undetermined, and the daemon would have refused to boot on essentially every machine. The safety property held (never falsely settled); the fix was unshippable. It passed my own tests because I had tested the *interesting* paths — PID reuse (live pid, wrong stamp) and cross-boot — and never a genuinely absent PID, the common case. The assumption underneath ("missing PID ⇒ ESRCH") was specific enough that I did not know I held it until I ran a probe binary against the platform. That is the generalizing failure mode for safety-critical code: attention goes to the exotic branches, the ordinary branch runs on an assumption nobody ever formed consciously.

**Verified while hardening the replacement** (same session, same method — check the platform, not the docs):
- `SysctlKinfoProcSlice` retries on ENOMEM when the process table grows mid-call (x/sys syscall_darwin.go:519-555) — it never returns truncation as success. But it DOES return `nil, nil` when the size probe reads zero — an empty table as a success — so an authority check (require your own `os.Getpid()` in the snapshot) is needed before treating absence-from-snapshot as proof; a process that provably exists and is missing means the enumeration proved nothing.
- `unix.Getsid(pid)` on darwin succeeds across sessions and across users (probed against a setsid'd same-uid child and root's pid 1) — POSIX permits an EPERM restriction there; darwin does not impose it, so session-membership scans do not silently drop members.

**Related pattern notes (lead's, post-ship)**: the converted-assertion and short-circuit test pathologies — this note's test gap is an instance of neither; it is the untested-ordinary-path gap.
